profile.behavior: Usually solitary; walks quickly along the water’s edge with a nearly constant tail-bobbing teeter, darts or probes for small prey, and flies low with rapid, shallow wingbeats alternating with brief glides.
field_marks: Small, forward-leaning shorebird with a rounded breast and body tapering to a longish tail
Straight bill slightly shorter than the head; orange with a dark tip in breeding plumage and paler outside breeding season
Dark eye accented by a pale eyebrow and narrow dark eye line
Brown to gray-brown upperparts; folded wings are long and a thin white wing stripe shows in flight
Breeding adults have bold dark spots across bright white underparts; nonbreeding birds are largely unspotted below
profile.habitat: Edges of fresh or salt water, especially rocky or pebbly shores, streambanks, rivers, ponds, lakes, marshes, beaches, mudflats, and estuaries; nesting areas combine shoreline, semiopen ground, and nearby dense vegetation.

findings: The candidate correctly depicts a breeding-adult Spotted Sandpiper: brown upperparts, densely spotted white underparts, orange bill with a dark tip, pale supercilium, dark eye line, longish tail, and slender flesh-yellow legs agree with the reference photographs and live identification sources.

The displayed length, weight, and wingspan exactly match Cornell's published ranges; Animal Diversity Web independently corroborates the 34–50 g weight and 37–40 cm wingspan. Audubon publishes a broader weight range and a slightly different wingspan range, reflecting source variation rather than an error in the plate.
All visible identification, plumage, habitat, and behavior statements are materially accurate. The common name, scientific name, and family are also correct.

The primary bird has one head, one beak, two legs, one tail, and the normal two-wing anatomy; only the near folded wing is visibly resolved in profile, while the separate lower-left wing is clearly an anatomical study rather than an extra appendage.

Minor anatomical clarity issue: the crossed feet make the toe arrangement difficult to parse, and the legs appear slightly elongated compared with several reference photographs, but there is no material deformity or incorrect limb count.

Minor composition issue: the vertical 0–20 cm ruler has no stated scale relationship to the horizontally posed bird, so it could be misread as a life-size scale. Labeling the plate “not to scale” or removing the ruler would improve scientific clarity.
